sections.guidingQuestion: Which event is an example of a gene-level substitution?
sections.explanation:
A gene mutation is a change in the DNA nucleotide sequence within a gene. A substitution replaces one base pair with another, an insertion adds one or more nucleotide pairs, and a deletion removes them. These changes can be small or substantial; it is the sequence alteration, not its benefit or harm, that defines a mutation.

A mutation in a protein-coding exon may alter codons, while a change in a regulatory or splicing sequence can affect when RNA is made or processed. Some DNA changes do not have an observable effect. Use the terms substitution, insertion and deletion before predicting consequences.

A DNA substitution changes one nucleotide pair; an insertion adds base pairs and a deletion removes them. The same category can be neutral or consequential depending on whether it affects a regulatory sequence, RNA splicing, a coding triplet or a protein active site. A mutation describes a sequence change, not a phenotype by itself.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why might a base substitution leave the polypeptide sequence unchanged?
sections.explanation:
A single-base substitution creates a different DNA sequence. If it changes a coding codon, the consequence may be synonymous (same amino acid), missense (a different amino acid) or nonsense (a stop signal), depending on the original codon and reading frame.

A single-nucleotide polymorphism is a variant at one nucleotide position that occurs in a population. Its history can involve substitution, but its existence does not establish that it is harmful. Degeneracy of the genetic code explains why a substitution may preserve a polypeptide's amino-acid sequence.

The genetic code is degenerate, so two codons can encode the same amino acid. A base substitution can therefore be synonymous, missense or nonsense in a protein-coding region, depending on the resulting codon. A single-nucleotide polymorphism describes variation at one genomic position and need not cause a disease.

A substitution changes a single DNA base pair. In the coding sequence, the resulting mRNA codon may still specify the same amino acid, may encode a different amino acid, or may become a stop codon. A changed amino acid matters most when it affects folding, an active site or another functionally important region; some substitutions have little detectable effect. Changes in regulatory DNA can alter gene expression without changing the polypeptide's amino-acid sequence. Therefore a mutated base does not automatically mean that the phenotype changes.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which coding change is most likely to produce a downstream frameshift?
sections.explanation:
The ribosome groups bases into successive non-overlapping triplets after the start codon. In a coding region, an insertion or deletion involving a number of bases not divisible by three changes the downstream reading frame, often producing many altered amino acids and an early stop. This is a frameshift.

An addition or removal of three nucleotides generally preserves the downstream triplet reading frame but adds or removes an amino acid. A large in-frame deletion can still destroy essential domains or folding, so being in-frame does not guarantee normal protein function.

An insertion or deletion of one or two bases inside a coding region generally shifts the downstream reading frame. An insertion/deletion of three bases may preserve the frame but still alter important amino acids. A premature stop can result from a frameshift, though outcomes depend on location and transcript processing.

Adding or removing one nucleotide in a coding region usually shifts the downstream codon reading frame, potentially changing many amino acids or introducing a premature stop. Adding or removing three coding nucleotides preserves the downstream reading frame but still changes protein length and potentially its function. Non-coding changes require a different analysis.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which is a biologically realistic source of mutation?
sections.explanation:
Copying errors can escape DNA polymerase proofreading, and DNA-repair mistakes can preserve a wrong sequence. Mutagens increase the likelihood of genetic changes: ultraviolet light can generate pyrimidine dimers, ionizing radiation can damage DNA, and some chemicals modify bases or interfere with replication.

A mutagen raises mutation risk but does not guarantee a mutation at a chosen gene. Mutation rates vary with exposure, sequence context and cellular repair. Damage to DNA is not yet the same as a permanent inherited change until it is fixed as an altered DNA sequence.

Replication errors and imperfect DNA repair introduce spontaneous mutations. Chemical agents can modify DNA bases, and ultraviolet or ionizing radiation can damage DNA in different ways. DNA repair systems lower mutation risk; detecting DNA damage is not proof that an unrepaired heritable base change has occurred.

Replication errors may arise spontaneously and persist if proofreading and repair fail. Ultraviolet radiation, certain chemicals and ionizing radiation can damage DNA and raise the probability of mutations, but they do not direct a useful change to a specific gene. If a mutation improves survival under a new pressure, selection may increase its frequency after it occurs. The environmental factor that causes DNA damage and the environmental factor that favours an allele may be different. Evidence of a mutagenic effect requires comparison with controls rather than assuming every exposed cell mutates.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which description best captures randomness in natural mutation?
sections.explanation:
Natural mutations arise without foresight about the traits an organism will need. They can occur in many parts of the genome, although some sequence contexts have higher mutation rates than others. Selection acts later on organisms with different variants; it does not instruct DNA to create a needed base change.

Antibiotic resistance illustrates this distinction: resistant bacterial variants may already exist before treatment, and exposure then favours their survival and reproduction. This does not mean that mutation rates are uniform, nor that mutagens have no effect.

Mutation is not a directed response to a species' needs. Some genomic sites mutate more frequently than others, but a new useful variant does not arise because an organism consciously requires it. Natural selection subsequently changes the relative frequencies of inherited variants when they affect survival or reproduction.

Mutations can arise through replication errors or DNA damage without being directed toward what an organism needs. An antibiotic does not instruct a bacterium to mutate into a resistant form: variants can exist or arise and then be favoured when susceptible cells are less likely to survive. Genetic sites need not have equal mutation rates, so 'random' does not mean all substitutions are equally probable. The occurrence of the mutation and the environment-dependent change in its frequency are different processes. This distinction is central to understanding mutation and natural selection.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which type of mutation can be inherited by biological offspring?
sections.explanation:
A mutation arising in a cell that contributes DNA to eggs or sperm can be passed to offspring. In contrast, a mutation confined to most somatic cells is transmitted only to that cell's mitotic descendants within the individual, not normally to the next generation.

Accumulated somatic changes in genes regulating proliferation can allow uncontrolled growth and contribute to cancer. A mutation in a skin cell after UV exposure does not mean the person's children will inherit that exact mutation. Inheritance depends on the cell lineage affected.

A variant present in an egg or sperm lineage may be transmitted to offspring. A somatic variant typically remains limited to that person's descendant cell lineage, although it can contribute to clonal expansion and cancer. A mutation is not necessarily beneficial or harmful just because of the tissue in which it appeared.

A somatic mutation becomes part of the descendants of the altered body cell after mitosis; it may form a localized patch of altered tissue or contribute to cancer. It is not normally transmitted to children because their nuclear DNA comes from gametes. sections.guidingQuestion: What is the ultimate origin of a novel allele?
sections.explanation:
Mutation is the ultimate source of new sequence variants and hence new alleles over evolutionary time. Sexual reproduction reshuffles existing alleles through meiosis and fertilization but does not itself create a novel nucleotide sequence unless mutation occurs.

Many new variants are neutral or harmful under current conditions; some can increase fitness in a particular environment. Natural selection alters allele frequencies over generations, and the benefits or costs of a variant can depend on genetic background and ecological conditions.

Mutation supplies novel alleles over evolutionary time; meiosis and fertilization mostly reshuffle alleles that already exist. Natural selection acts on phenotypic effects of inherited variation and may increase or decrease an allele's frequency. Distinguish the generation of variation from sorting of variation.

Natural selection needs heritable variation to produce an inherited population response. Mutation creates novel nucleotide sequences and can therefore introduce previously absent alleles to a gene pool. Meiosis and fertilization mainly recombine alleles that already exist, creating new genotypes rather than new gene sequences. A new allele may be lost by chance, remain neutral or become common under selection. Distinguish the appearance of a mutation in one cell from an increase in its frequency across a population over generations.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is a gene-knockout organism useful?
sections.explanation:
A gene knockout deliberately disrupts a gene so that it no longer provides its usual functional product. Researchers compare knockout organisms or cells with appropriate unmodified controls and ask which features differ. Knockout libraries in some model species allow the effects of many genes to be investigated.

A knockout phenotype is evidence that the gene contributes to the measured trait under the test conditions, not proof that the gene acts alone. Other genes may compensate, and a lethal knockout may prevent observation of later functions. The guide does not require memorizing knockout production techniques.

Disabling a gene can reveal its contribution to phenotype by comparing knockout and otherwise comparable wild-type organisms. Changes in other genes or developmental compensation can obscure a simple one-gene/one-trait inference; appropriate controls and replication are essential. Detailed knockout methods are not required in this IB understanding.

Researchers compare organisms or cells with a functional gene against otherwise comparable material in which that gene has been deliberately rendered inoperative. A lost function can provide evidence that the original gene contributes to a particular process, such as pigment production. However, little visible effect need not mean the gene is useless: another gene might compensate, or a phenotype may appear only under certain conditions. The official requirement is the logic and use of gene knockouts, not the laboratory details of constructing a knockout.

sections.guidingQuestion: What role does guide RNA serve in a typical CRISPR–Cas9 editing system?
sections.explanation:
In engineered gene editing, a guide RNA directs Cas9 to a complementary DNA target adjacent to an appropriate recognition motif. Cas9 can cut the target DNA; cellular repair can introduce insertions or deletions, while other editing configurations may achieve specified sequence changes. Off-target edits, incomplete editing and variable repair outcomes require assessment.

Casgevy uses CRISPR–Cas9 edited patient blood stem cells targeting a regulatory enhancer of BCL11A. Reduced BCL11A in erythroid cells increases fetal hemoglobin, benefiting some people with sickle cell disease or transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia. This is a regulated ex vivo intervention, not evidence that arbitrary disease-causing variants can be safely repaired throughout the body.

A common CRISPR–Cas9 editing design uses guide RNA for target recognition and Cas9 to cleave DNA near a target adjacent to a suitable recognition motif. Cellular repair can disrupt the gene or enable a designed edit, but outcomes can include unexpected insertions/deletions and off-target changes. A successful therapy for one condition does not establish universal safety or germ-line acceptability.

Guide RNA specifies a complementary DNA target near a suitable adjacent recognition motif; Cas9 cuts it. Cellular repair then determines the sequence outcome. Error-prone repair may disrupt the gene, while precisely specified changes generally require additional strategies. Confirm edited sequence, possible off-target changes and measured phenotype separately rather than inferring successful editing from cleavage alone.

sections.guidingQuestion: What can help explain a highly conserved sequence?
sections.explanation:
Conserved nucleotide or amino-acid sequences remain similar across populations or species, sometimes over long evolutionary intervals. One explanation is functional constraint: changes disrupt an important product, so purifying selection removes many altered variants from populations.

Some regions may also accumulate fewer changes because their local mutation rate is lower. Shared ancestry, selection and regional mutational processes all affect observed conservation. Comparing aligned sequences is evidence, but a conserved sequence does not by itself prove what precise molecular function it performs.

Conservation means that related sequences remain alike over evolutionary time. Functional constraint and purifying selection can explain similarity because damaging variants are removed; locally lower mutation rates are an alternative hypothesis. Sequence similarity alone cannot distinguish these explanations without more evidence.

Comparative sequence observations can show that sites are conserved across taxa. Functional constraint is a plausible, testable hypothesis, while shared ancestry and local mutation rates also shape conservation. Establishing the specific function of a conserved sequence requires further experimental or comparative evidence.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "Every SNP changes the amino acid of the encoded polypeptide." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: Synonymous substitutions are possible because multiple codons can encode an amino acid. A single-base substitution creates a different DNA sequence. If it changes a coding codon, the consequence may be synonymous (same amino acid), missense (a different amino acid) or nonsense (a stop signal), depending on the original codon and reading frame. Changing the mRNA codon GAA to GAG preserves glutamate, whereas GAA to GUA changes glutamate to valine.
markingPoints: The genetic code is degenerate, so two codons can encode the same amino acid
A base substitution can therefore be synonymous, missense or nonsense in a protein-coding region, depending on the resulting codon
Correct the common inference: Synonymous substitutions are possible because multiple codons can encode an amino acid.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "All insertions and deletions cause an identical frameshift." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: The reading frame shifts when the net nucleotide change is not divisible by three. The ribosome groups bases into successive non-overlapping triplets after the start codon. In a coding region, an insertion or deletion involving a number of bases not divisible by three changes the downstream reading frame, often producing many altered amino acids and an early stop. This is a frameshift. Deleting one coding nucleotide may alter every downstream triplet, but deleting three bases may preserve the later reading frame.
markingPoints: An insertion or deletion of one or two bases inside a coding region generally shifts the downstream reading frame
An insertion/deletion of three bases may preserve the frame but still alter important amino acids
Correct the common inference: The reading frame shifts when the net nucleotide change is not divisible by three.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "A mutagen deliberately rewrites a chosen gene to improve survival." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: Mutagens create damage or increase error rates without purposeful targeting. Copying errors can escape DNA polymerase proofreading, and DNA-repair mistakes can preserve a wrong sequence. Mutagens increase the likelihood of genetic changes: ultraviolet light can generate pyrimidine dimers, ionizing radiation can damage DNA, and some chemicals modify bases or interfere with replication. UV-induced DNA damage in skin cells may become a stable mutation if copying or repair fails.
markingPoints: Replication errors and imperfect DNA repair introduce spontaneous mutations
Chemical agents can modify DNA bases, and ultraviolet or ionizing radiation can damage DNA in different ways
Correct the common inference: Mutagens create damage or increase error rates without purposeful targeting.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "Bacteria anticipate antibiotics and intentionally mutate the exact resistance gene they need." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: Mutation is not directed toward a beneficial outcome; selection changes variant frequencies. Natural mutations arise without foresight about the traits an organism will need. They can occur in many parts of the genome, although some sequence contexts have higher mutation rates than others. Selection acts later on organisms with different variants; it does not instruct DNA to create a needed base change. A pre-existing resistant bacterium can outgrow susceptible bacteria after an antibiotic is applied.
markingPoints: Mutation is not a directed response to a species' needs
Some genomic sites mutate more frequently than others, but a new useful variant does not arise because an organism consciously requires it
Correct the common inference: Mutation is not directed toward a beneficial outcome; selection changes variant frequencies.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "Every cancer-associated mutation is automatically passed to the next generation." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: Somatic mutations generally stay within the organism; germ-line mutations can be inherited. A mutation arising in a cell that contributes DNA to eggs or sperm can be passed to offspring. In contrast, a mutation confined to most somatic cells is transmitted only to that cell's mitotic descendants within the individual, not normally to the next generation. An inherited pathogenic variant may originate in a gamete precursor, whereas UV-related skin mutations are generally somatic.
markingPoints: A variant present in an egg or sperm lineage may be transmitted to offspring
A somatic variant typically remains limited to that person's descendant cell lineage, although it can contribute to clonal expansion and cancer
Correct the common inference: Somatic mutations generally stay within the organism; germ-line mutations can be inherited.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "Meiosis produces new DNA base sequences solely by independent assortment." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: Independent assortment rearranges existing alleles; mutation creates new sequence variants. Mutation is the ultimate source of new sequence variants and hence new alleles over evolutionary time. Sexual reproduction reshuffles existing alleles through meiosis and fertilization but does not itself create a novel nucleotide sequence unless mutation occurs. A novel bacterial resistance allele can spread when antibiotics select for carriers, while often offering no advantage without the drug.
markingPoints: Mutation supplies novel alleles over evolutionary time; meiosis and fertilization mostly reshuffle alleles that already exist
Natural selection acts on phenotypic effects of inherited variation and may increase or decrease an allele's frequency
Correct the common inference: Independent assortment rearranges existing alleles; mutation creates new sequence variants.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "A knockout result proves that a gene is the sole cause of a complex trait." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: A controlled knockout suggests gene function but requires interpretation and replication. A gene knockout deliberately disrupts a gene so that it no longer provides its usual functional product. Researchers compare knockout organisms or cells with appropriate unmodified controls and ask which features differ. Knockout libraries in some model species allow the effects of many genes to be investigated. A yeast knockout lacking a nutrient-synthesis enzyme grows only if the missing nutrient is supplied.
markingPoints: Disabling a gene can reveal its contribution to phenotype by comparing knockout and otherwise comparable wild-type organisms
Changes in other genes or developmental compensation can obscure a simple one-gene/one-trait inference; appropriate controls and replication are essential
Correct the common inference: A controlled knockout suggests gene function but requires interpretation and replication.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "Every CRISPR cut produces the precise planned DNA replacement without errors." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: A directed cut permits editing, but repair outcomes and clinical safety require testing. In engineered gene editing, a guide RNA directs Cas9 to a complementary DNA target adjacent to an appropriate recognition motif. Cas9 can cut the target DNA; cellular repair can introduce insertions or deletions, while other editing configurations may achieve specified sequence changes. Off-target edits, incomplete editing and variable repair outcomes require assessment. An ex vivo Casgevy treatment edits the patient's own harvested blood stem cells and returns them after conditioning.
markingPoints: A common CRISPR–Cas9 editing design uses guide RNA for target recognition and Cas9 to cleave DNA near a target adjacent to a suitable recognition motif
Cellular repair can disrupt the gene or enable a designed edit, but outcomes can include unexpected insertions/deletions and off-target changes
Correct the common inference: A directed cut permits editing, but repair outcomes and clinical safety require testing.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim "All conserved sequences must have an identical mutation rate and an experimentally proven function." using a mechanistic explanation and a suitable biological example.
questions.answer: Purifying selection and lower local mutation rates are alternative or joint hypotheses. Conserved nucleotide or amino-acid sequences remain similar across populations or species, sometimes over long evolutionary intervals. One explanation is functional constraint: changes disrupt an important product, so purifying selection removes many altered variants from populations. A catalytic residue conserved in related enzymes suggests that substitutions there often reduce enzyme performance.
markingPoints: Conservation means that related sequences remain alike over evolutionary time
Functional constraint and purifying selection can explain similarity because damaging variants are removed; locally lower mutation rates are an alternative hypothesis
Correct the common inference: Purifying selection and lower local mutation rates are alternative or joint hypotheses.
